subtopic: MB. REID-FIGURES AS TO RAILWAY PASSES, GIVEN IN DEBATE ON MAY 6

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MB. REID-FIGURES AS TO RAILWAY PASSES, GIVEN IN DEBATE ON MAY 6
speechtext:
I rise to what I believe to be a question of privilege. On Tuesday last I made a speech in this house in which I gave the house certain figures as to the number of railway passes issued in Canada. In the Ottawa Citizen of May 7 there appears an article in which it is reported to be stated by high officials of the board of transport commissioners that the figures quoted by me are not quite correct.

I take strong objection to the board of transport commissioners or any official issuing a denial of a statement made by me, or any other hon. member, especially when no member of this house can get the information from the board. If any contradiction is to be made I suggest that the minister in charge give instructions to the board that members of parliament be allowed to obtain information to w'hich I believe they are entitled.

"opposed", I 'have the right to express my mind on the principle of the bill and tell the house why I oppose it. That is quite clear, and I hope that you will sustain me in that, Mr. Speaker, before I go further.
The hon. member for Temiscouata was not in the house when we started on these bills-
Let us begin again.

At that time I stated that the terms of the resolution passed by the house yesterday was that bills to which no opposition was taken should go through automatically and be disposed of, but that if objection were taken to any bill, that made it an opposed bill within the meaning of the resolution and it would go to the foot of the list. I suggest to the house that our present procedure is lacking in dignity.
I think the house ought to dispose of these unopposed bills en bloc, as proposed, and then proceed to deal with the other bills on which there is to be some discussion. Of course I am in the hands of the house; we can take each bill separately, which will be in accordance with the rules; but I suggest that our proceedings this afternoon have been marked by a great lack of dignity, which I should not like to see continue longer. Perhaps there may be other suggestions as to how we should proceed with regard to these bills.

I do not think anyone desires to delay the house unduly, but there are times when it becomes necessary to make some effective protest regarding the procedure being followed. This, I take it, is what some of us. for various reasons, are bent on doing to-day. It was suggested by you, Mr. Speaker, that if these bills were opposed they should stand over. I am not opposed to the principle of granting a dissolution of an unhappy marriage, but I am opposed to dealing with these bills in the present manner. So far as I am concerned, since a number of these bills have been placed at the end of the list, I think we should treat them all alike. I do not mind whether they are taken together or separately, but I believe every bill is going to be opposed on the grounds I have mentioned.
May I say very respectfully, Mr. Speaker, that in my opinion your rulings are invariably fair; but I think we would be making a mistake if we permitted to go unchallenged the proposition that we may do no more than rise and indicate opposition to a bill, without giving reasons for that opposition. I believe that if we oppose or support something, we should have the right to say why
Divorce Bills

we do so. As I say, I do not wish to see the business of the house held up. I think a fairly effective protest has been made this afternoon against the procedure at present being followed, so perhaps the bills might now be taken together and considered as opposed bills. I should be glad, if necessary, to make a motion to that effect.
The whole procedure has become a farce.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, perhaps the best course would be for Your Honour to ask the house if there is any person who dissents from the procedure that has been suggested; that is, that all the divorce bills be dealt with together. Then perhaps some hon. member will say that he desires to discuss each of these bills. That being so. they become opposed bills and go to the foot of the list. That procedure will take only a very few minutes of our time, and will dispose of all these bills. I do not think any motion is required to do that. The only thing necessary, it seems to me, is the suggestion that these bills be put to the house all together. Then if someone says he desires to have something to say on each of these bills, immediately they go to the foot of the list.
Mr. O'NEILL:	I should like to say a
word in connection with the fiasco which has taken place in the last few minutes. We have in the gallery this afternoon a number of children, who will leave here with absolutely no respect for the House of Commons after the spectacle they have witnessed to-day.
Included in this list of bills is one about which I should like to say a few words; I am not at all satisfied with the answers that have been given so far with respect to it. As the procedure has been developed this afternoon, however, if I rise in my place to ask a question I am presumed to be opposed to the bill. I do not wish to be placed in the position of being accused of opposing something I know nothing about, but that is the position in which I find myself to-day. If we follow the suggestion just advanced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley), if I rise to say a word when we come to the bill about which I wish to speak, it is presumed that I am opposed to it. If I just say "opposed," that does not constitute a speech; but the moment anyone tries to make a speech there are cries of "order" from all 
over the house. I should like to know just where we will end up if we adopt the suggestion of the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the whole trouble arises from the concluding words of the motion adopted on Wednesday, with regard to giving precedence to unopposed bills. This has not been understood. I would suggest that by unanimous consent the house might overlook the last few words of that motion and proceed with the bills on the order paper in their numerical sequence. That will not be doing any injustice to anyone; we can go through the list and dispose of the bills one by one. Let us go back to order No. 1 and go right through the list as it appears on the order paper.

If I may
be permitted a word, Mr. Speaker, for the last several minutes I have been trying to think of a solution to the impossible situation into which this house has got itself this afternoon. My friend the clerk assistant of this house, with his literary turn of mind, recalled to me that Cromwell once characterized parliamentary procedure as a tortuous and ungodly jumble. If that was ever exemplified in the twenty years I have been around this house, it was this afternoon. Let us be sensible men and extricate ourselves from this position. Let us not have it said that this house has lowered itself to a position in which it becomes the laughing stock of the country, for that is what we are doing this afternoon.
We are sensible men. Let us review the position de novo. I am of the opinion that the suggestion advanced by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) is perhaps the logical one to accept, and I am going to ask the house to adopt that suggestion unanimously. Take each of these bills in its regular sequence and either pass it or reject it. Begin again, and forget about the motion that was adopted on Wednesday. I agree with the minister that the whole difficulty arises from the construction that has been placed on the last few words of that motion. I have no doubt in the world that the Prime Minister's intention w'as good, that he desired to expedite the business of the house, but that has not been the result. Let us, as sensible men in a deliberate assembly, start again and deal with these bills as they appear on the order paper.

Is it the intention of the
minister that we should start at order No. 1 again?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe I had the floor when the proceedings were interrupted by Your Honour's ruling to the effect that this was an opposed bill. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) having moved an amendment to the motion for second reading, it is now in order for me to make a few observations.
What is the position with respect to this bill? It is this, that in advancing their particular financial theories the government of Alberta is desirous of establishing in Canada-and it is not limited to Alberta especially-a bank, under the provisions of the Bank Act. That is their object. They will attempt to set up as a department of the provincial government of Alberta a bank to carry on, with certain limitations, the business of commercial banking in Canada. I believe that is a fair statement of their position. They will operate not as individuals but as a government department with, I assume, share capital owned by the province of Alberta, but expressly reserving and restricting certain of the operations of the general provisions of the Bank Act so that it will not have reference
to or cover the institution they hope to incorporate.
I do not intend to debate to-day their theory of monetary reform, nor do I intend to enter into any controversy in that regard. But I do suggest that we cannot agree to the principle of giving the approval of the house to a provincial government's doing indirectly that which it cannot do directly. I lay that down as a principle, and I do not think I should have to argue it. That whole matter was threshed out at great length last session in the committee on banking and commerce. Careful consideration was given to it. I am not going to advert to the discussion which took place in that committee, much of which I believe was perhaps foreign to the bill under discussion at that time. Much time was consumed-I shall not say wasted-on that occasion in an examination of the theories of social credit.
I believe the procedure followed by the government of Alberta is entirely wrong. If they proceed in a proper way and according to the laws of our country, as they are bound to do, I am not opposed to the sponsors of the theory of social credit asking that a charter for a bank be conferred upon certain gentlemen who as individuals represent their particular financial viewpoint. I am, however, opposed to the method of procedure under which they undertake to operate. I will say to them that if members of the Alberta government-Mr. Aberhart and Messrs. A, B, C, D and E-will come to this parliament and, by petition, ask for the incorporation of the Alberta Provincial bank, or a bank known by some other name, on the theory that when they get a charter they will be in a position to put into effect the theories they are sponsoring in Canada to-day, I shall support them, and give them an opportunity to demonstrate, if they can, once and for all, that social credit is a sound monetary theory.
If I have read aright the statement of a former Minister of Finance, Mr. Dunning, it would seem that he conceded the idea that these gentlemen might be allowed to proceed to demonstrate the soundness of their theory, if they would conform to the general laws of the country. They have never seen fit to do so. But if they will come forward and seek to incorporate a bank, in conformity with the general laws laid down by parliament, which have been revised every ten years since we have had a Bank Act, I will vote for the charter, and let them demonstrate what they can do, provided, always, that they comply with the provisions of the Bank Act and provided, further, that they put up the necessary funds. That should not be difficult because the amount is not large. The province
Alberta Provincial Bank

could then pass enabling legislation permitting it to invest its own funds immediately in the shares of the bank. But the applicants must conform to the general laws of the country in so doing, and unless they do so I cannot support the principle of this measure. Certainly it is not the measure I have attempted to visualize.
This bill sets out the establishment of a bank, as a department of government in Alberta, and I suggest that the Minister of Finance ought not to allow it to go through in that form, or even in the manner he has suggested. I cannot congratulate him upon his courage. He has a definite responsibility to the people of Canada to see that the general laws of the country are carried out, and at the very threshold he must meet the underlying principle. He has not met it. He seeks, as did his predecessor, to side-step that responsibility and to have the bill go to a committee, on -e theory that it will be reported back to the house in a condition so emasculated that the promoters will not accept it. I do not conceive that to be the proper duty of the government in the premises. If the government will not take a definite stand, at least I am going to take a stand as to what I believe should be done, and let it go at that.
I have no doubt the amendment will carry. It is a government amendment, and in the very nature of things, and by virtue of the operation of the House of Commons, it will carry. I suggest, however, that the method suggested by the minister is not the proper one.
I am not going to discuss at length the sections in the bill. I say to these gentlemen that they have no right to come to the House of Commons and urge that restrictions which must be imposed upon me or my associates, if I come here asking for a charter for a bank, shall not be imposed upon them. Why are the restrictions in the Bank Act placed there? They are placed there for the protection of the public, the protection of the depositors and the shareholders. These restrictions have been in force for a long period of time, and, if you accept the principles contained in the Bank Act you will agree that experience of the past fifty or sixty years has shown them to be good.
To-day the sponsors of this bill are trying to get out from under the responsibility placed upon them by the general laws of the country. I cannot accept that procedure. If they want to have a bank, and all the advantages of a bank operating under the Bank Act of Canada, then let them at the same time accept the responsibilities imposed

by the Bank Act upon those who seek to carry on business with the public.
There are a good many other arguments I could adduce against the bill. My hon. friend the proposer of the measure, the member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), has suggested that this bill would be an aid to the war effort of Canada. He did not elaborate on that theme.
I could have done so.

I doubt
very much if he could have. I wish he had, so that we could have examined it to see what its foundation was.

I can prove it to
you.

My hon.
friends are strong on assertions but mighty short on proof. I do not intend this afternoon, nor do I intend on any future occasion, to get into an argument or an altercation as to the value of social credit. I have been hearing it for twenty years. I have interviewed Major Douglas and all the other proponents of this strange philosophy, but I am still unconvinced, and I think I shall remain that way. I suggest to these gentlemen that they have started wrong, that they are still on the wrong road. I think I gave them some advice last year, which did not cost them anything; I suggested that if they would come back to the house at this session with a bill in the standard form and ask as individuals for the incorporation of a bank, that I would do what I could in my very limited way to forward their proposal. But not on the basis of this bill.
I think we ought to decide on the principle of this bill here and now and not send it to a committee. Is there any hon. member of this house who does not visualize what will happen if this bill goes to the banking committee? In a large measure we will have a repetition of what happened last year. Without question there will be repetition, although I would hope that it would not go on so long. Does any one suggest that the bill will come back with the recommendation that it become law? If it does, then I say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) that the responsibility will be laid on his doorstep. This is a responsibility which he ought to assume now. As the head of the treasury, as the man charged with the responsibility of seeing that the banking laws of this country are carried out, he ought to say here and now whether he approves the principle of the bill. I cannot understand the attitude of the government, and I did not understand it last year. If their purpose was simply to pass

Alberta Provincial Bank
the buck from the government to the members of the banking and commerce committee, then it had that result. But I do not think that is the way in which a government ought to met its responsibility. I am not absolving the government in any degree; I think it must assume responsibility. It should not sidestep a decision with regard to the principle involved in this bill; it ought to meet the question squarely. If it does not meet it now, it will have to meet it when the bill comes back from the committee, assuming that it passes the committee.
Let the gentlemen who want this bill come to parliament just as you or I or any other citizen of this country would come who thinks he can carry on a bank. Let them come and produce a bill in the form contemplated by the Bank Act, and let them be ready to assume all the advantages, as well as the responsibilities that will accrue to them. They should not try to relieve themselves from the responsibilities. If they act on this suggestion I will support a measure so produced and give them a chance to demonstrate the fallacy or otherwise of their financial philosophy.
I am opposed to the second reading of this bill and intend to vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, I do not agree with some of the views just expressed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). I am of the opinion that this petition for a bank charter is properly made to parliament as such, and ought to be considered by parliament. Parliament should not expect or ask the government to decide what parliament should do. The petition is to parliament, and parliament must decide on the merits of this particular request. I do not agree with the view that the provincial government ought not to be entitled to a charter to inaugurate and operate a provincial bank. I cannot see why that should not be done.

It is
against the law.
I hear the leader of the opposition interject that it is the law.

Against
the law.

The law is that they cannot do it? If that is so then it seems to me that the provincial government has the right to come before this parliament and present its petition. If the law does not allow the provincial government to obtain a charter for a bank, parliament should be advised, and when the time comes the Bank Act should be amended to give it that power.
I am not persuaded that the law is prohibitive as the leader of the opposition suggests. I am of the opinion that the suggestion made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) that this matter should go to the banking and commerce committee is sound. That is the proper procedure to follow. But I agree with the leader of the opposition in expressing the hope that the procedure followed this year will be different from that which was followed last year.
Because I was a member of the committee dealing with the defence of Canada regulations I was unable to be present at many of the meetings of the banking and commerce committee, but I was present at some of them, and it seemed to me that the discussion, or the major part of it, had nothing to do with the merits of the bill. During the few times I attended I found that the committee was holding an inquisition of the Alberta government, its financial ideas, and particularly of the policies pursued by the provincial treasurer, who was a witness before the committee. I hope that this year the bill will be considered on its merits.
I believe it would be an excellent thing if our provinces had the right to operate provincial banks. Of course they would be publicly-owned institutions. While I would prefer to see the present banking system taken out of private control, yet as long as parliament will not do that I think a good case can be made for publicly-owned institutions in our provinces.

With safeguards under
the Bank Act.

With safeguards under the Bank Act. If the present bill does not conform to the law of the land, I am not arguing that it should be adopted and recommended by the committee without amendments. We have been told by our friends to the left that the banks have certain powers which enable them to create credit, and so on. If the banks have that power, and if a charter is granted to the province which comes within the four corners of the Bank Act, it seems to me that our soc-'al credit friends would then have the power do all the things which they claim the present banks can do.
I have not gone into the details of this bill. Like the leader of the opposition I did not know that it was to come up first this afternoon. As a matter of fact I thought that Bill No. 27, respecting British Columbia Telephone Company, was to come up this afternoon as the first order of business.
I think we should consider the request of the leader of the Social Credit group, the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), that
Alberta Provincial Bank

the bill be referred to the committee, that it be examined there as it ought to be, and that it be reported back to this house. If it is against public policy and the law of the land, then the house cannot adopt the bill until the law is changed.

Does the hon. member realize that this is the same bill as was submitted last year? It is the same, word for word; there is no change. It is the same bill. It was examined carefully last year and is being reintroduced this year. Does the hon. member understand that?

I must say that I did not expect this bill to come up this afternoon. I had not compared it with the bill of last year and therefore I cannot say that I knew it was the same bill. I understood there were some changes. But that does not alter the fact that the Social Credit group in this house or the government of Alberta have the right to reintroduce the bill and to ask for its examination by the committee. The committee would have the right to report as it sees fit, differently or in the same terms as last year. I am simply supporting the motion that this bill be referred to the committee where it can be thoroughly examined. If a charter within the four comers of our Bank Act were granted to the province of Alberta, the government of that province would have the opportunity which it says it now lacks to demonstrate its monetary theories and its policy.
The hon. member advocates that, notwithstanding the fact that the officers of the crown advised that such a bill last year was unconstitutional.

I am not saying that. I am saying that if a charter within the four corners of our Bank Act were recommended by the committee, then if parliament refused to grant the charter, the government of Alberta would immediately and properly say: We cannot do the things we wish to do and which the private banks can do under their bank charters. But if a charter within the four corners of our Bank Act were granted to a provincial bank of Alberta, the government of Alberta would have to demonstrate that their monetary theory was sound within the present financial system. The whole of the criticism that has been levelled against existing financial institutions by the advocates of social credit, is that the private banks have the power to create credit and to do the things which the province of Alberta wishes to do but cannot do without a bank charter. If they were given the same power as the banks, no more and no less, they would have the same opportunities of doing the same things. That is the
rMr. Cold well.]
point I am making, and I therefore strongly support the motion that this bill and the petition be referred to the committee.

Mr. Speaker, the leader of the opposition has mentioned the Bank Act, which was considered by the banking and commerce committee in 1934. I was not a member of the committee at that time but I have made a very exhaustive study of the evidence that was given before that committee. The leader of the opposition said-I have forgotten his exact words, but what he meant was that we were trying to do something in a roundabout way. Everyone who will take the trouble to read the evidence that was taken before the committee on banking and commerce in 1934 must admit that the committee, with one or two exceptions, and certainly the leader of the opposition was not one of those exceptions, did not realize that the banks create all the money that they lend, a fact which the present Minister of Finance admitted in this house within the last month when he said that if the government borrows from the banks $250,000,000, that is a clear addition of $250,000,000. And yet that plain fact is said to be just a theory held by this group! It is not a theory at all of any group. It is a fact, and no one who knows anything about it can successfully deny that fact. It was only two years ago that the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Towers, was a witness before the banking and commerce committee, and I asked this question of him in the committee: "Do you agree that the banks lend money by creating the means of payment?" And the answer he gave was, "Yes, that is correct. There may be other ways of putting it, but that is correct."
I am sure that the committee on banking and commerce in 1934, when the present Bank Act was passed, never realized that the banks create the money which they lend. I am quite sure that that fact is not realized by the majority of members of this house at the present time. We in this group are credited with having peculiar monetary ideas and theories. It is contended that we want to do something which has never been done before. Why, it was only yesterday or the day before that an hon. member, speaking to the amendment to the budget which the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), had moved that parliament, which is sovereign in its power, should issue the money which is required to make up the gap between government revenue and expenditure, likened that proposal to rubbish money. Think of it, money which bears the stamp of the King likened

Alberta Provincial Bank
to rubbish 1 Money which is issued by a private corporation and bears the photograph of a private individual is sound money, while the King's money is unsound! Could disloyalty go further than that? Could absurdity go further than that? Could anything be farther from the truth? Why should we in this group be accused of having peculiar monetary theories when we state that the banks create the money that they lend? There is not the slightest doubt but that that is the fact, and anybody who denies that fact to-day is either dishonest, or incompetent, or both.
It is proposed to refer this bill to the committee on banking and commerce. The leader of the opposition appears to be frightened at that. I do not suppose for a moment that the bill will pass the committee. It seems to me that the leader of the opposition is frightened that during the discussions of the committee some vital facts which have been carefuly hidden hitherto may come to light. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has stated, this is a petition to parliament, not to the government, and therefore I hope the house will send this bill to the committee on banking and commerce, where it can be considered on its merits.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before the house is not concerned with the merits of this bill, nor has it anything to do with the merits of the theory of social credit. The motion is that the subject matter of this bill be referred to the banking and commerce committee. I remember quite well another occasion when the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation spoke in this house in favour of a bill which he had introduced to make it illegal to prevent men from joining a labour organization or trade union, and the government took the position that while it was in sympathy with the principle of the bill, it could not proceed with it because it was beyond the constitutional power of parliament. The officers of the crown, having declared last year that this bill in its present form is unconstitutional, will, I assume, so declare now.
Not necessarily. They changed their minds with reference to the decision on the constitutionality of discrimination against men joining unions.
That may be, but I am assuming that their opinion still stands. .
That is a pure assumption.
And I believe that any lawyer would be satisfied that the bill in its present form is unconstitutional.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should say that that is doubtful. I do not remember the express terms of the opinion, but I believe there was a great deal of doubt about the matter last year.
The law officer of the crown quite definitely stated that the bill was unconstitutional.
One man's opinion.
Well, of course, an opinion must be the opinion of one man.

One man cannot
decide a case.
I was speaking of an officer of the crown.
He expressed a great deal of doubt.

My understanding and my reading of the remarks are certainly as I have stated. The Minister of Finance has expressed some doubt in the matter, and that perhaps weakens the argument I was going to put forward, namely, that if he felt as I did, how could he answer the argument of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) that the position of the Minister of Finance was, not that he lacked courage, but that he should, in face of the fact that the bill was unconstitutional, take the position that the time of the banking and commerce committee should not be wasted, and that he should simply say that, the bill in its present form being unconstitutional, the matter should be dropped until such time as the bill was brought within the ambit of a proper constitutional arrangement. That is the point I take in respect to this matter, without offering at this time any comment one way or the other as to the merits of the proposal.

The
hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) gave an unfortunate illustration of his point. His own statement nullifies his argument. He used the illustration that some years ago the then member for Winnipeg North Centre, the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group, brought before this house a bill to provide against discrimination against men seeking to join trade unions. At that time the contention was that the matter was not within the jurisdictional powers of parliament. I remember that the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Bennett, contended that it was; and the following year the government brought in legislation to implement the very suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

No.

Alberta Provincial Bank

They brought in amendments to the criminal code to provide for the very thing that he mentioned in his bill. The mere statement that this matter cannot be discussed again, and cannot be referred to the committee on banking and commerce again, because some official of the crown gave some opinion-which is only an opinion-last year as to its constitutionality, would hardly warrant this house in precluding further discussion of it.

Before
this motion is put to the house, may I observe that, when this matter was before the banking and commerce committee last session, the committee reported to the house without making any motion for concurrence, and this automatically prevented any hon. member from discussing its contents. I recall that I asked on two occasions after the report was presented whether the chairman of the committee intended to move concurrence in the report. The last time I asked the question the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) responded that it was not always necessary to move concurrence. The result was that the report was not discussed by this house in any way, shape or form.
It does seem to me that, if parliament itself has been requested to grant a charter to this bank, parliament itself should be free to discuss the details of the report of that committee. One of the things I desired to mention at that time, but which I was deprived of the privilege of mentioning, was the very point which has been mentioned this afternoon -the advice which was given that perhaps the bill was unconstitutional.
May I suggest this: the record will show that Mr. Varcoe was brought before the committee and that he was given a very limited time-I do not know how long, but I believe his evidence can be read in fifteen minutes, certainly in half an hour-but I doubt very much whether he submitted evidence as to the constitutionality of that particular bill.
Will the hon. gentleman permit me?
Yes.

I have before me the minutes of the standing committee on banking and commerce. At page 117 Mr. Varcoe, to whom the hon. gentleman has just made reference, concludes by saying:
That is to say that while parliament has complete power over the subject of banking it cannot impose upon a provincial government the powers of legislation as would be the case if this bill were passed, because the members will realize that the directors of the bank and

the lieutenant-governor in council, under paragraph 3 (c), would acquire subordinate legislative power in respect of banking.
Then he goes on to give the reasons why he regards this bill as being unconstitutional- two reasons with which I do not need to burden the house. So that the decision was quite definite.

My impression is simply this, that Mr. Varcoe was suggesting that this parliament could not grant a charter for a bank to a provincial government; that his argument was not as to whether this bill was constitutional, but whether it was constitutional for parliament to grant a charter for a bank to any government. However, my suggestion may be open to question. The least one can say is that while Mr. Varcoe did give evidence for a short space of time, no one would say that his evidence was conclusive. The only way in which it could be proved to be unconstitutional would be to have it brought before the proper courts, which, of course, has not been done.
While it is true that Mr. Varcoe was a law officer of the crown, it is quite possible that some other witness whose reputation was just as good might have been brought in, and who could be furnished with just as sound arguments as Mr. Varcoe, to present the other side of the picture. But this was not done.
The hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Ross), I believe it was, interjected a while ago, the suggestion that the bill in its present form had not been changed from the form in which it was presented to parliament last session. While I would not offer my opinion as an authority, one reason why we support the motion that the bill be sent to the committee is that should any clauses in it fail to meet with the approval of the committee it can be considered whether amendments should be made in the committee stage. Often that is where amendments to certain sections are made. The fact that the bill in its present form is the same as it was last session is no indication that the sponsor of the bill would not consider amending certain sections of it.

There is no desire on the part of the sponsor or of the people who petitioned for this bill to do anything which is unconstitutional or contrary to the banking laws of Canada, either in law or in effect. I do not propose to reopen the debate which occurred earlier this afternoon: I think a sufficiently effective protest was made against the form of procedure. But I want to state explicitly that in my opinion Canada should follow the example of all other civilized countries, where unhappy marriages may be dissolved by the courts, by nullification by an ecclesiastical authority, or through some method of granting relief under certain circumstances.
If this were not a war session, with the business we have ahead of us, I think I would follow the procedure adopted by the leader of our group some years ago in this house and ask for a discussion on each of these divorce bills. I feel that the procedure followed here is against the best interests of the parliament of Canada, and that this is a matter upon which some public opinion should be encouraged, shall I say, to the end that a change might be made. I do not agree with the procedure, but I am not going to offer further opposition to these bills at the present time.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I think, Mr. Speaker, it would be an ideal situation if we could avoid having divorce bills come to parliament, but I ask my hon. friend to consider that there is a very substantial body of religious opinion in this country which is absolutely opposed to divorce. In our neighbouring province of Quebec that opinion is in the majority; the
Divorce Bills

people of that province who hold that view are opposed to the establishment of any forum or tribunal to which would be given jurisdiction to deal with this kind of litigation, if I may use that term in respect of it. On the other hand there are people in that province, citizens of this country, who are entitled under the laws of .Canada to have the bond of matrimony dissolved if they so desire; it is not against their convictions. Since the province will not establish any forum, or give jurisdiction to the courts of that province, these people are perforce obliged to come to parliament; no other jurisdiction is open to them.
So long as that is the situation I think parliament will have to exercise its jurisdiction in connection with matters of this kind, much as I personally would prefer to see them referred to the courts. We shall have to perform our duty whether we like it or not, and consider bills of this kind. But I would hope that in the future-personally I do not see any possibility of it-the happy time will come when legislation of this sort will disappear from the order paper. It is not possible at the moment; it may never be possible. Having regard to that, then, I think we should exercise the jurisdiction conferred upon us by the constitution and give proper consideration to bills of this kind.
I know nothing about these bills, and I am not going to read them or inform myself in connection with them; nor am I going to enter into a discussion as to their merits. I should like to say, however, that I know the gentlemen in the other place who compose the committee on divorce, and I think they perform their functions conscientiously. It may be that they are not as thorough as a court of law would be, though sometimes in courts of law they issue these decrees with what seems to me rather undue haste. I have had some experience in connection with divorce matters; it all depends on the judge who tries the cases. As a rule, however, I think the senate does the work just about as well as it is done in a court of law. We must face the inevitable; the constitution gives us the jurisdiction, and we must exercise it if people ask us to do so.

Last
year a group of several hon. members on this side of the house protested to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who was in his seat at the time, with regard to the whole procedure in reference to this matter. At that time the Prime Minister said consideration was being given to working out some other procedure, but so far nothing has been done. It is true, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) has said, that since

certain provinces are not prepared to set up divorce courts the only way these people can get divorces is to come to this parliament. We are not quarrelling with that. What we are quarrelling with is that members of this parliament are being made parties to certain acts, with the facts concerning which they are not familiar.

In just
what way are they being made parties?

The leader of the opposition asks me in what way. He is being asked, as I am, to vote on these bills. I am not familiar with the details concerning them. I am not able to say whether these divorces ought to be granted or ought not to be granted. It is impossible to study all the evidence. Just a little over a year ago in this very district a private detective was sent to gaol because it was proved that he had been a party to collusion in a number of divorce cases. We do not know to what extent there has been collusion; we have no information at all as to what provision is being made for the children. Last year we drew to the attention of the Prime Minister one case in which a divorce was granted because one of the contracting parties had a social disease. Yet the very bill granting that divorce contained a provision that the parties might remarry! Thus we were turning loose on society a person who, according to the evidence heard before the committee which recommended the divorce, was suffering from a social disease.
It is our feeling that if parliament is to accept this responsibility it ought to delegate these matters to some judicial or quasi-judicial body, assisted by social service workers, which would have at hand the necessary facilities, first, to investigate thoroughly these cases, and, second, to see that provision is made that no children shall suffer as a result of the granting of a divorce.
Does the hon. member suggest a retrial in the commons? There has been one trial already before the senate committee.

No, I am not
suggesting that. I am suggesting that the government consider setting up a dominion court, or that the power to go into these cases be delegated to a judicial or semijudicial body.

We could not do that. The procedure in these matters is vested in the provinces; but the subject matter, which is marriage and divorce, under the constitution is vested in parliament.

Divorce Bills

As I said a moment ago, I think that could be got around
by setting up a quasi-judicial body. There is no reason why a committee of judges should not be set up, who would examine these cases and send on their recommendations to this parliament. We have that every day under the defence of Canada regulations; the recommendations of a judge or group of judges come back to this parliament. A committee of judges would be much more competent than a committee of the house to sift this information. For the last five years I have served on private bills committees that have gone over these cases; for the last two years I have served on standing orders committees which have had to decide whether bills coming in late should be received by the committee, and I want to express myself as absolutely dissatisfied with this procedure. If parliament is to accept this responsibility it must carry it out in a proper manner and make sure that the cases are thoroughly investigated. If we are not prepared to do that we should not grant divorces at all. We should do one thing or the other; as it stands at the present time the system is a disgrace. It makes a farce of a sacred institution. By casting our votes for these divorces, about which we know little or nothing, we may be turning children loose in the world under the control of some parent who is irresponsible and incapable of supporting them properly. We know nothing about these details, and I for one am not prepared to give my support year after year to a procedure which is farcical in the extreme.
As I have said, last year we made an appeal to the Prime Minister. Now I should like to express the hope that the Minister of Finance, who is leading the government in the house at the moment, will give heed to the suggestion that some procedure other than that now followed be worked out for the handling of divorce bills. Either we grant them, after thorough investigation and after complete assurance that all possible provision is made for the children affected, or we do not grant them at all. Let us not accept responsibility unless we are prepared to discharge it humanely.

I think the whole matter was placed clearly before the house by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). He stated the matter succinctly, but I doubt if the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) was exactly fair in his presentation, when he suggested that we deal with this matter in the way in which other countries do. He and every other hon. member know full well there is only one reason why the
House of Commons deals with the matter at all; and until he comes forward with a solution, I suggest that in all kindness it is unfair to have it said that the time of parliament is being wasted, and that he and others of his group are in favour of some other system of dealing with this serious problem.
I differ with the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas). Just why one requires a judicial body to deal with divorce is beyond me. We have here a jury of good men and true, and the question is purely one of fact. Every hon. member knows that if he so desires he may appear before the divorce committee and obtain any information he wishes in the matter. The situation should be placed fairly before the house.
Like every other hon. member, I do not like the present procedure of dealing with divorce cases, but until we have a solution of the one burning question which affects an entire province, I am content to carry on in the way in which we are doing.

I would only reiterate what I said before, namely, that I am not opposed to divorce. I believe there are situations in which it is justified. Scripture says: "Be not unequally yoked together." I would not suggest a procedure such as is followed in the country to the south of us, where a man or a woman may obtain a divorce from his or her helpmate for some childish or trivial reason, and call it cruelty, or something of that kind. It may be said that the wife would not allow the husband to take so many lumps of sugar in his coffee, or something of that sort. Under certain circumstances, I think divorce is a wise procedure. I believe, however, that before the final decree is issued, every effort should be made to reconcile the parties.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) has stated that it is necessary to give relief to people living in Quebec, where the legislature appears to be unwilling to pass the necessary provincial laws. Those people have a right to be protected. But when it comes to procedure in parliament which, of course, includes action by both houses, I support the suggestion of the leader of the opposition that it ought not to be necessary to have two courts. As the senators are worthy and reputable men-and most of them are men of long experience-why not have one court, and put the full responsibility on them. Under those circumstances they would know that they would be wholly responsible. We have at present a sort of divided procedure. They may be a little careless or a little lax, and say, "Oh wrell, if any injustice is being
Divorce Bills

done, the lower house will remedy it." But if they knew their decision was final, as in the case of the civil courts, possibly they would take more care, and would see that wise decisions were made. Also they might appoint a committee to interview the people concerned and see if a reconciliation might be brought about. Sometimes parties can be convinced to come together again and, unquestionably, that is much better than dividing the family. We see that done quite commonly in the United States where, on occasions, people remarry more than once. They may marry, obtain a divorce, remarry, sometimes divorce again and remarry again. The fact that they look at divorce in that light and trivial way is some indication as to why we should be more particular in our handling of the matter.
Speaking earlier this afternoon, I referred to the importance to be attached to the disposition of the children. It must be decided which of the parents is to have them, no matter which is guilty, because it is not always the guilty one who is the cause of the divorce. There is such a thing as provocation by a bullying husband or a nagging wife, but the decision must be made as to which one is better able to take care of the children. One of the cases before the house this afternoon was a case in which seven children between the ages of three and ten years were involved. What is to become of them? That is a matter which should be given the greatest consideration. No consideration is given to it in the other house; they do not have to. The law does not require it, but I say that some care should be taken. If the older people make wrecks of their lives, that is no reason why they should be permitted to wreck the lives of their children, who should be brought up under decent conditions.
I believe, however, that the principle of divorce should be carried out, with all due precautions. As the leader of the opposition has suggested: Why have two courts? Why not have only one, and place full responsibility on it? We find that if full responsibility is placed at one point, greater care is taken than if it is shared. When there is a division of responsibility, someone is always passing the buck to somebody else and saying, "Oh, well, it is going to the other chamber, anyway."
Question.

Is it the pleasure of the
house that we pass all these divorce bills?
I thought they were to be taken separately?

On division.

Mr. NEILL; Have we not heard that enough times this afternoon, and was there not a motion by the Minister of Pensions and National Health, that these bills were to be taken one by one? What is the matter with the procedure, that it cannot be followed in the ordinary way? After wrangling about it for an hour, we agreed that we should start at order No. 1 and go right through the bills, one after another. But not more than ten minutes have elapsed until we start to deviate from that position. I protest most emphatically. I ask the Minister of Pensions and National Health if he does not support my statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes, that was done.

Mr. F. P. WHITMAN (Mount Royal) moved the second reading of Bill No. 31, for the relief of Dorothy Jean Fletcher.
Mr. Speaker, I ask the sponsor of this bill to tell us if there are any children resulting from this marriage, their ages, and any provision which has been made for their care.

Mr. Speaker, I am
perplexed at the interest which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has taken in this bill. The evidence produced before the committee on divorce states that this woman was married in 1926, lived with her husband for about one year and did not see him again for about fifteen years. One child, a boy, was born, and he is now about thirteen years of age. After this man had tried to enlist in the army it was found that he had been living with another woman, two children having been born to this woman. In reply to the hon. member for Temiseouata (Mr. Pouliot) I Should like to say that this

Divorce Bills
case is one which could be read by anyone. There was nothing dirty or filthy about the case at all; it was simply one of absolute
desertion.
Who has the child?
The child is with the mother.

Mr. Speaker, I could not reply to the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) on the other bill, so that I shall take this opportunity of doing so.
We are not lightly criticizing this procedure. The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) suggested that it might be possible to devise a method which would be more satisfactory, even though the province which will not set up a court of its own continues to hold to that position. The hon. member for New Westminster suggested that any member of this house could* go to the senate committee dealing with these petitions and get all the information he required*. That may be true, but, as the hon. member knows, it would be almost impossible for any one of us to spend that much time in the senate committee. I doubt if he can tell me the particulars regarding any one of these bills. I know I could not.
I think the suggestion made by the hon. member for Weyburn is sound. He suggested that if we are to continue to deal with these matters, and apparently we shall have to do so as long as one province objects to granting relief under its own jurisdiction, then a judicial committee should be set up which could sift the evidence and go into the merits of the cases. I have an alternative suggestion to make. I suggest that we set up a national committee, a personal relations committee as it were, which could look into these cases before they come to us here. As a matter of fact, in several of the states of the United States they have committees of this description. Frequently it has been possible to prevent the parties from going through with a divorce; a reconciliation has been effected and they have agreed to live together again. I think we could devise ways and means of getting around the objectionable practice we follow here. I remember one year I was a member of the private bills committee and the agriculture committee. On one occasion I was asked to absent myself from the agriculture committee for a few minutes because they had not a quorum in the private bills committee. It was toward the end of the session, and it was necessary to give approval to some eight bills. Much to my dislike and over my protests, those bills went through in about ten or fifteen minutes. It is true the senate committee had gone thoroughly into the bills, but I do not think any hon. member of this house should be asked, without more information than is available to us at the present time, to assume the grave responsibility of breaking up a home, and, as has been pointed out, perhaps doing something which may not be beneficial to the children of the marriage. The suggestion made last year when similar matters were under consideration should be followed, namely, that the government should be asked to devise some method which would protect the home.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I do not think the suggestion of delegation of authority is feasible. I have a constructive suggestion to make to the government. In England they have an official known as the king's proctor. Very often in cases like these he intervenes. I suggest to the government and to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that one of the officials of the Department of Justice, or, if they are too busy, some reputable counsel, be appointed as king's proctor to attend the meetings of the senate divorce committee and crossexamine the witnesses. He could assist in preventing collusion and in establishing the truth of any incriminating evidence. Thus a safeguard would be provided in connection with divorce legislation.
In New Brunswick they do not have a king's proctor, but every judge presiding over a divorce court constitutes himself, some more and some less, as a king's proctor. He intervenes and cross-examines the witnesses, especially if he has reason to believe that there is collusion. I admit that it is not a satisfactory way to handle the matter, because a judge cannot do anything more than crossexamine the witness. He must take the answers of the witness, whatever they may be. But a king's proctor can test the credibility of the witnesses. In England, the intervention of the king's proctor has prevented the granting of decrees.
It has in this province, too.

I think
that is a partial solution to the problem to which hon. gentlemen to my left are referring.

I
endorse the suggestion of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). If we had such an official as a king's proctor I am sure that many of these bills would never reach this house. It is a notorious fact that there is collusion in a third if not more of these cases. I have them all here, and in nine-tenths of the cases the procedure is the same. A man goes to the hotel desk and registers for himself and the woman with him, and there happens to be a man standing at his elbow who is
Divorce Bills

able to swear a few weeks later that he saw him register. You cannot always have a coincidence like that. It is ridiculous to ask us to believe that there is not collusion in these cases. I remember one celebrated case in England many years ago where the king's proctor intervened. As I say, if we had such an official here there would be fewer divorces granted.

The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said that he doubted that the member for New Westminster had read all the evidence. I can tell him right now that he is quite correct. It is surprising the lack of information that is sometimes displayed in the house regarding these bills, and the amount of information which is to be heard in the corridors. My attention was drawn to one bill, and I think something should be done about it. I do not think it is right to allow people who have been in the country only two years to obtain a divorce on evidence which is just hearsay.
Which one is that?

I have not the bill before
me, although I have it in my office, but if I remember correctly it is Bill No. 36. I think careful note should be taken of that case.

I have just one word more to say with reference to what the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) has said. For three or four years while I was a member of the private bills committee I read the evidence in connection with these bills religiously year after year. I felt it was my duty to do so as a member of that committee. It became perfectly clear to me that many of these divorces were the outcome of collusion. They almost all followed the same pattern. You could have changed the names, and the evidence in one case would have fitted all the others. Personally, I became so disgusted that I could not conscientiously act on that committee during another session, and that is why I made an appeal to the house to consider getting a more satisfactory procedure for handling these bills.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to endorse the suggestion of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). In a United States newspaper which I picked up a short time ago, I found an article on this very subject. It showed that one woman had acted as co-respondent in New York in 500 cases and that she was paid a professional fee. The province of Quebec is not very far from New York, and I am suspicious about the bona fides of many of these divorces. We

pass them lightly when they need to be carefully probed into. I think the house will do well to pay heed to the suggestion made by the hon. leader of the opposition.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to interject another suggestion, entirely different from the ones that have been advanced here this afternoon. I know that many members will not agree with what I am about to say. I am going to suggest that the principal in the case who is the guilty party and has been the one responsible for the crime should not be permitted to marry again. I know, of course, that this would involve a revision perhaps even of some of our provincial laws, but I am certain that if such a thing were written into the laws of this country there would be fewer divorces.
I am going to suggest, too, that the crime which is committed in these cases and the result of which is divorce is an age-old crime, and I doubt whether the nation will ever get rid of that crime through a system of legislation such as we have to-day. I might suggest that religious organizations have a duty. Should I go so far as to say that some of our churches have perhaps not paid enough attention to the teaching of such doctrines as the sanctity of the home? At the root of this evil lies the fact that our people are not sufficiently concerned with the tremendous implications involved in the crime which calls for divorce, or in the sanctity of the home, the number of homes being torn to pieces by divorce, and the children of divorced parents having to retain the stigma of their parents having committed such an act of infidelity.
All these things enter into the picture. The matter goes deep. I might go further and say that perhaps there is some reason for our believing that with such looseness in our marriage laws we shall not be able to build a healthy and a God-fearing nation. I say that this matter goes very much deeper than most people suspect, and if our laws were revised so that those who were guilty of the crime were not permitted to marry again, it might not be far from the truth when I say that there would be far fewer divorces in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I sat as a member of the private bills committee for the first time last year and voiced my part in the feeble protest against the manner in which these bills were being pushed through. I was at a loss to understand why we should allow such a farce to continue. After the bills had passed the private bills committee they were brought in here, and we went on record as passing thirty-six divorce bills in about twelve minutes.

Divorce Bills
Under the British North America Act, divorce is made a matter of federal jurisdiction, and I suppose that so long as that condition continues we shall suffer under this burden, but seven provinces of this dominion have already accepted divorce as a provincial responsibility and relieved us of the shame of passing these bills in the way we do.
I should like to support what has just been said by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) who joined with me in a protest against the way in which these bills were being pushed through. But we were unable to get any action at all in the private bills committee in having the question of social disease brought up. The thing that appalled me was the fact that we went on record, first of all, as dissolving a marriage, and then immediately granting the right to the divorced people to marry again. It seems to me that national health alone should be sufficient grounds for us to voice our objection to such procedure, and perhaps if we block these bills continuously in this house it will have the desired effect of getting the two remaining provinces to establish their own divorce courts. I think that would be a step in the right direction. I refuse to be a party to condoning the way in which divorce is now being handled in this parliament, and I shall continue to do so whenever the matter is brought up here.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to enter into any discussion of the moral grounds for granting divorce or of whether there is collusion in the divorce cases brought before this parliament. The last speaker has said that this debate may do much towards impressing the people of Canada with the necessity of having two of the provinces establish divorce courts such as we have in the other provinces of this dominion. I do not often disagree with what he has to say; but I do think-and in saying this I believe I represent the viewpoint of members generally-that a time like the present with the empire in peril is not the time to worry about divorces and the necessity for a change in our present method of granting divorce.
I am a new member here, but this afternoon has been to me an experience which I hope I shall never have again. Are we, Mr. Speaker, so out of tune with reality that we spend our time in connection with matters such as this? The unrealism of this afternoon has made almost a caricature of this parliament and this house.
We tried to straighten it out, though.

The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) says that we tried to straighten it out. Yes, but let us straighten it out after this war is over: let us no more- and I dislike speaking in this way-while this war is on devote ourselves, in the manner we have this afternoon, to matters which are so insignificant compared to those of greater moment.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.
